issues.subcategory: inconsistent units / unit error
issues.description: The text reports wheel speed in m/h (meters per hour), which is physically implausible for a wheel descending a ~1-meter track in seconds. A speed of 123.6 m/h would mean covering 1 meter in ~29 seconds, contradicting the gravity-driven descent of a wheel on a 14-degree incline. The unit is almost certainly meant to be something else (e.g., m/min or cm/s), and the 'generation slope' estimate of 5.37 m/h is reported in the same units as absolute speed (145.7 m/h), which is internally confusing. This pervasive unit ambiguity undermines interpretation and replication.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed produced by first generation participants on their last trial was 123.6 m/h (95% Highest Posterior Density Interval: (117.3, 130.6))

issues.subcategory: optimization percentage does not match reported values
issues.description: The claim of '71% optimization' is not reconcilable with the reported numbers without an undisclosed baseline. If first-generation speed is 123.6 and final is 145.7 with a maximum of 154, the increase (145.7-123.6=22.1) relative to the gap to maximum from baseline (154-123.6=30.4) is ~73%, but this depends on an unstated MinSpeed/starting reference. The MinSpeed in the payoff equation is 96 and MaxSpeed is 160, yet the 'maximum possible speed' is stated as 'about 154,' creating a discrepancy between the payoff-anchoring constants (160/96) and the empirical optimization calculation. The derivation of 71% is not shown.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: contradictory framing of preregistered hypothesis 2 result
issues.description: The text states no substantial support for theory transmission affecting understanding, yet simultaneously reports a Generation x Treatment credible interval of (0.03, 0.81) that excludes zero — which by the authors' own stated inference rule (95% credible intervals to make inferences) constitutes evidence for an effect. The narrative ('barely changed,' 'slightly better') downplays a result that meets the authors' own significance criterion, an inconsistency in how the inference rule is applied.
issues.quote: participants in the very last generation had a slightly better understanding when they had inherited a theory (Treatment 95% CI: (-2.54, 0.31), mean = -1.14; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (0.03, 0.81), mean = 0.44, Figure 2.B). Thus, these analyses do not provide substantial support for the idea that the transmission of explicit causal theories affects wheel optimization and individual understanding.

issues.subcategory: exploratory analyses presented without correction or preregistration
issues.description: The central mechanistic findings (theory coding effects on exploration and understanding, the subgroup analyses of balanced/unbalanced wheel producers) are explicitly labeled exploratory but are presented as strong conclusions ('strongly affected,' 'striking differences'). The post-hoc grouping of Configurations participants into three categories (various/balanced-only/unbalanced-only) involves undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom (how 'only' was defined, thresholds) and no multiple-comparison adjustment, inflating Type I error risk for the headline mechanistic claim.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants’ exploration behavior (Supplementary Figure 1).

issues.subcategory: severely underpowered subgroups
issues.description: Key conclusions about theory-type effects rest on tiny subgroups: only 6 participants inherited a 'full' theory, 15 an inertia theory, 17 a centre-of-mass theory. Conclusions about the exploration and understanding patterns of these subgroups (especially the 6-person full-theory group, described as producing 'compact and asymmetrical wheels') are drawn from samples too small to support reliable inference, yet are presented in Figure 3 and discussed as substantive findings.
issues.quote: The few participants who inherited a full theory (N = 6) produced compact and asymmetrical wheels (D-H).

issues.subcategory: understanding measure may capture exploration history rather than reasoning
issues.description: The authors' own analysis demonstrates that the 'understanding' test score is confounded with what configurations participants explored (balanced-only producers score better on inertia, etc.). This means the test does not cleanly measure causal understanding as a stable cognitive construct, but partly reflects induced observation history. This undermines the central claim that 'understanding did not improve,' since the measure conflates reasoning ability with exposure to particular stimuli.
issues.quote: These results suggest that the understanding patterns observed in participants who received unidimensional theories is likely the result of the canalizing effect of theory transmission on exploration.

issues.subcategory: performance-neutral claim not directly tested
issues.description: The claim that the canalizing effect of unidimensional theories is 'performance-neutral' because better understanding of one dimension compensates for worse understanding of the other is asserted but not formally demonstrated with a performance comparison across theory-type subgroups. Given the underpowered subgroups, a null performance difference could reflect low power rather than true neutrality, and the compensation argument is theoretical rather than empirically established.
issues.quote: Note that in the present case, this canalizing effect is performance-neutral: with our 2-dimensional problem, better understanding of one dimension and worse understanding of one dimension simply compensate each other.

issues.subcategory: extrapolation from low-dimensional task to complex technologies
issues.description: The conclusions extrapolate from a deliberately simplified 2-dimensional optimization problem (20,736 configurations, 5 trials) to highly complex cumulative technologies like bows and kayaks and to archaeological inference about ancient cognition. While the authors call the low-dimensionality 'conservative,' the inference that causal understanding is unnecessary for real-world cumulative technological evolution is a substantial overclaim given the artificiality and constrained search space of the task.
issues.quote: our experiment indicates that one should be cautious when interpreting complex archaeological materials as evidence for sophisticated cognitive abilities (such as reasoning, problem-solving or planning), since these abilities are not the sole driver of technological sophistication

issues.subcategory: WEIRD sample limitation
issues.description: The entire sample consists of French university students (a WEIRD, formally physics-educated population), yet broad claims about human technological evolution and ancestral cognition are made. The authors acknowledge this in passing regarding cross-cultural exploration but still draw species-level conclusions. The selective, non-random exploration the authors attribute to good intuitions may itself be a product of Western formal education, which they cannot rule out.
issues.quote: we asked successive ‘cultural generations’ of participants (French university students) to optimize a physical system

issues.subcategory: no blinding of conditions or analysis
issues.description: The experimenter manually positioned weights and was aware of conditions, and data analysis was explicitly not blind to condition. Although the experimental program automated timing, the lack of blinding (combined with the experimenter being an author who performed the experiment) introduces risk of expectancy effects, particularly in the theory-coding interpretation and exploratory analyses.
issues.quote: Data analyses were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments. No data points were excluded from the analyses.

issues.subcategory: handling of failed (non-descending) wheels
issues.description: Wheels that did not descend were assigned a speed of 0, while the descriptive speed lines and HPDIs are computed for 'non-failure wheels.' This dual treatment (0 for some analyses, exclusion for descriptive averages) is inconsistent and not fully justified. Assigning 0 to failures is an arbitrary imputation that can strongly distort linear model estimates of generation slopes, and the number/distribution of failures across generations and treatments is not reported numerically.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0. Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.

issues.subcategory: deviation from preregistered analysis 4 due to non-convergence
issues.description: The preregistered model for understanding (analysis 4) did not converge, so the authors aggregated scores and dropped the 'Physical Principle' terms. This deviation collapses precisely the inertia-vs-centre-of-mass dimension that turns out to be central to the exploratory mechanistic story, and the decision to aggregate is a researcher degree of freedom prompted by the data (negative correlation discovered post hoc). The change should be flagged as potentially affecting the headline 'understanding did not change' conclusion.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: convergence/sampling problems acknowledged but not fully resolved
issues.description: For Analysis 3, the authors report inefficient chains and low effective sample size for a parameter, addressing it only by 'running additional models' described in supplements. Reporting a primary inferential model with known sampling pathology and relegating the robustness checks to supplementary tables makes it difficult to evaluate whether the treatment/interaction credible intervals are trustworthy.
issues.quote: For this model, the chains were inefficient and the effective number of samples for one parameter was low (see Supplementary Table 3).

issues.subcategory: priors and model specification not reported
issues.description: The Bayesian multilevel models are described only at the level of outcome/predictor/random-effect structure. No priors, likelihood specification, number of chains/iterations, warmup, Rhat, or effective sample sizes are reported in the main text. Without these details the Bayesian credible intervals cannot be evaluated or reproduced, which is essential for a Bayesian analysis.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32.  Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33 and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.subcategory: theory coding reduces rich written theories to binary categories
issues.description: Participants' free-text theories (up to 340 characters) were collapsed into four coarse categories (inertia/centre-of-mass/both/neither). This operationalization may misclassify partially correct or nuanced theories and discards gradations of theory quality. The 'irrelevant/diverse' bin (18 of 56) is heterogeneous and undefined, lumping qualitatively different theories together, which weakens the construct validity of 'theory type' as a predictor.
issues.quote: 15 inherited an inertia-related theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass-related theory, 6 inherited a full theory and 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories.

issues.subcategory: discrepancy in N for no-theory group
issues.description: Figure 3 states that participants who did not inherit any theory number N=70 (the full Configurations treatment), but the Configurations treatment includes first-generation participants who received no social information at all and others who received configurations. Elsewhere subgroup Ns (15+17+6+18=56) correspond to non-first-generation Configurations+Theory participants. The mixing of N=70 (Configurations) versus the theory-inheriting subgroups creates an apples-to-oranges comparison (no-theory group includes generation-1 participants and config-only learners), which is not clearly reconciled.
issues.quote: Participants who did not inherit any theory (N = 70) sampled various positions along each spoke (A)

issues.subcategory: confound between configuration and theory information content
issues.description: In the Configurations+Theory treatment, participants received an additional channel of information (the theory) on top of configurations, but were prevented from transmitting specific configuration performance. This asymmetry in available information across treatments means any null difference could reflect a trade-off (more theory but restricted score-sharing) rather than a true absence of theory effects, confounding the clean comparison the authors intend.
issues.quote: Participants could not transmit information about the performance of a specific configuration in order to prevent individuals from extending the number of transmitted configurations as compared to the “Configurations” treatment.

issues.subcategory: task may not capture 'cumulative' cultural evolution
issues.description: Only the last two configurations and their scores are transmitted across single-trial overlapping generations of 5, and improvement plateaus near ceiling within 5 generations. This rapid near-ceiling optimization in a small finite space may reflect simple hill-climbing/social-learning of good configurations rather than the open-ended cumulative cultural evolution the framework invokes. The conceptual mapping between this constrained search task and cumulative technological culture is not fully justified.
issues.quote: these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: intuition interpretation from non-random exploration
issues.description: The inference that participants 'had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration' from the observation that wheels clustered in the upper-right quadrant is a causal/cognitive interpretation of an aggregate behavioral pattern. This pattern could equally arise from social transmission of early successful configurations rather than individual intuition, and the design cannot distinguish these, yet a cognitive claim is asserted.
issues.quote: This indicates that participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration, and sampled the parameter space fairly efficiently in that regard.

issues.subcategory: sample size justification absent
issues.description: The authors state no statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes, justifying 14 chains only by comparison to prior literature. Given the central inferential claims rest on credible intervals (including null-effect interpretations of treatment differences), an absence of any power/precision analysis makes it impossible to assess whether null findings reflect true absence of effects or insufficient sensitivity.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications30,31.

issues.subcategory: null result interpreted as evidence of no effect
issues.description: The headline claim that causal understanding is 'not necessary' and that theory transmission 'has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution' rests on credible intervals that include zero (e.g., generation slope for understanding CI (-0.34, 0.25)). Interpreting a wide interval spanning zero as positive evidence of no effect (absence of effect vs. failure to detect) is an over-interpretation, especially given small samples and acknowledged sampling problems.
issues.quote: Moreover, we find that the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution.

issues.subcategory: 'understanding' test format may underestimate knowledge
issues.description: The understanding test uses forced binary/ternary predictions on 10 fixed pairs presented in the same order to all participants. A score of ~4.5/10 hovers near chance, but the fixed item set and order, plus the all-or-nothing nature of the items, may not validly capture graded or implicit understanding, and order effects are uncontrolled (no counterbalancing), threatening the validity of the central 'understanding' construct.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.subcategory: sex-segregated chains as uncontrolled design factor
issues.description: Chains were sex-segregated (exclusively male or female) but sex is never entered as a factor in the analyses, nor is the rationale for segregation explained. If performance or understanding differs by sex, segregation confounds chain-level random effects with sex, and the failure to model or report sex effects is an unexamined design choice.
issues.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one condition of the experiment and one sex-segregated chain.

issues.subcategory: rater reliability reported but coding adjudication unclear
issues.description: Five raters coded theories with reported Cohen's kappa (0.81, 0.85), but kappa is a pairwise statistic and it is unclear how five raters produced a single coefficient or how disagreements among five raters were adjudicated into final categories. The procedure for resolving discrepancies and assigning final theory categories is not described, affecting reproducibility of the key 'theory type' variable.
issues.quote: Cohen’s kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters (0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).

issues.subcategory: payoff incentive may bias exploration toward exploitation
issues.description: Participants' rewards depended on both their own and the next participant's performance, and they received the predecessor's best two configurations. This strongly incentivizes copying/exploiting inherited good configurations rather than exploring, which inflates apparent rapid optimization and could itself suppress the development (and hence measurement) of understanding. This incentive structure is a design feature that confounds the interpretation that understanding 'fails to improve' as a cognitive rather than motivational result.
issues.quote: their reward depended both on their own performance and on the performance of the next participant in the chain

issues.subcategory: misalignment between 'wheel dynamics unfamiliarity' citation and sample
issues.description: The justification that the task is unfamiliar cites a study showing Western students poorly understand wheel dynamics, yet the same study's findings about reliable systematic misconceptions could mean participants bring strong (mis)intuitions rather than a blank slate. Treating the system as one where participants 'cannot rely on acquired knowledge' is partly contradicted by the later claim that participants had 'appropriate intuitions' about acceleration, an internal theoretical tension.
issues.quote: it is unfamiliar (cognitive studies show that western students have poor understanding of wheel dynamics 15), so participants cannot rely on acquired knowledge to solve the task.
